proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(E_0\) for expectation under \(P_{0,O}\), put \(u=J^{-1}\mathbf 1_J\), and let \(\mu_{C,t}(x)=(\mu_{2,t}(x),\ldots,\mu_{J+1,t}(x))^{\prime}\).  We first establish identification rather than building it into the observed-law functionals.  No anticipation gives \(Y_t=Y_t(0)\) for \(t<T\), and every donor is untreated at \(T\).  Under parallel trends,
\[
 \delta_1^0(x)=\Delta\mu_g(x),\qquad g=2,\ldots,J+1.
 \tag{1}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_F[Y_T(1)-Y_T(0)\mid G=1,X=x]
 &=\mu_{1,T}(x)-\mu_{1,T-1}(x)-\delta_1^0(x)\\
 &=\mu_{1,T}(x)-\mu_{1,T-1}(x)-u^{\prime}D(x).
\end{aligned}
 \tag{2}
\]
The overlap condition gives \(\pi_1\ge\kappa_0\epsilon_0>0\), so averaging (2) with the well-defined treated-stratum weights
\[
 \nu_x=\frac{p_X(x)p_1(x)}{\pi_1}
 \tag{3}
\]
proves \(\theta(P)=\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_O)\) on \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PT}}\).  Under the synthetic-mean restriction, the preperiod equations and the intercept equation give \(a(x)=B(x)w(x)\), hence \(\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}w(x)=1\).  The rank assumption gives \(\lambda_{\min}(B^{\prime}B)\ge\kappa_0>0\), so the displayed formula uniquely identifies \(w(x)\).  Its final-period equation gives
\[
 E_F[Y_T(0)\mid G=1,X=x]=w(x)^{\prime}\mu_{C,T}(x).
 \tag{4}
\]
Thus subtraction from the observed treated final mean and averaging with (3) proves \(\theta(P)=\theta_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_O)\) on \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SC}}\).  In particular, the two observed-law functionals agree at every \(P_0\in\mathcal M_I\) because each equals the causal target there.

We next prove that the two influence-function faces actually meet.  For one stratum define
\[
 \psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)=g_{\mathrm{PT},x}+R_{\mathrm{PT},x}^{\prime}a,
 \qquad
 \psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)=g_{\mathrm{SC},x}+R_{\mathrm{SC},x}^{\prime}d.
 \tag{5}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}tangent\text{-}normal\text{-}form}\), sums of the first family in (5) exhaust \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\), and sums of the second exhaust \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)\).  Here is an explicit compatibility argument which includes the derivative of the identified synthetic weight.  Suppress \(x\) and the common factor \(\nu_x\) temporarily, and write a dot for a pathwise differential at \(P_0\).  Since
\[
 \operatorname{range}(A_{\mathrm{PT}})=\{v\in\mathbb R^J:\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}v=0\},
\]
adding a PT normal permits every donor weight \(v\) satisfying \(\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}v=1\).  The resulting conditional-mean differential is
\[
 L_{\mathrm{PT}}(v)
 =\dot\mu_{1,T}-\dot\mu_{1,T-1}
  -v^{\prime}(\dot\mu_{C,T}-\dot\mu_{C,T-1}).
 \tag{6}
\]

At an exact SC restriction, differentiation of the full-rank least-squares formula gives
\[
 \dot w=(B^{\prime}B)^{-1}B^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B\,w).
 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently, the unrestricted SC differential is
\[
 \dot\mu_{1,T}-w^{\prime}\dot\mu_{C,T}
 +q_0^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B\,w),
 \qquad
 q_0=-B(B^{\prime}B)^{-1}\mu_{C,T},
 \tag{8}
\]
and \(B^{\prime}q_0=-\mu_{C,T}\).  The SC restriction normals add exactly the vectors in \(\ker(B^{\prime})\).  Hence the SC affine face consists of the expressions
\[
 L_{\mathrm{SC}}(q)
 =\dot\mu_{1,T}-w^{\prime}\dot\mu_{C,T}
  +q^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B\,w),
 \qquad B^{\prime}q=-\mu_{C,T}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Let \(e_0\in\mathbb R^T\) select the intercept row and let \(e_-\in\mathbb R^T\) select the row for period \(T-1\).  At the intersection, (1) supplies a scalar \(\delta_x\) such that
\[
 \mu_{C,T}=\mu_{C,T-1}+\delta_x\mathbf 1_J.
 \tag{10}
\]
Because \(B^{\prime}e_0=\mathbf 1_J\) and \(B^{\prime}e_-=\mu_{C,T-1}\), the vector
\[
 q_*=-e_- -\delta_x e_0
 \tag{11}
\]
satisfies the constraint in (9).  The intercept rows of \(a\) and \(B\) are fixed, so \(e_0^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B\,w)=0\).  Substituting (11) into (9), and using the preperiod matching equation, yields
\[
 L_{\mathrm{SC}}(q_*)
 =\dot\mu_{1,T}-w^{\prime}\dot\mu_{C,T}
  -\dot\mu_{1,T-1}+w^{\prime}\dot\mu_{C,T-1}
 =L_{\mathrm{PT}}(w).
 \tag{12}
\]
The derivative of the stratum weight \(\nu_x\) is also common: the two conditional contrasts have the same value at the intersection, so their product-rule terms involving \(\dot\nu_x\) coincide.  Restoring these terms and the factor \(\nu_x\), equation (12) gives a representer having both forms in (5).  This proves, stratum by stratum, that
\[
 \mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\cap\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)\ne\varnothing.
 \tag{13}
\]

For any coefficients \((a,d)\), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}union\text{-}qp}\) and the definition of \(h_x\) give
\[
 \psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)-\psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)=c(a,d)^{\prime}h_x.
 \tag{14}
\]
Since \(\Omega_x\) is positive semidefinite,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Omega_x^{1/2}c(a,d)=0
 &\Longleftrightarrow c(a,d)^{\prime}\Omega_xc(a,d)=0\\
 &\Longleftrightarrow
 E_0[\{\psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)-\psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)\}^2\mid X=x]=0.
\end{aligned}
 \tag{15}
\]
Thus the QP constraint is exactly equality of the two stratum representations in \(L^2(P_{0,O}\mid X=x)\), while its objective is
\[
 E_0[\psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)^2\mid X=x]
 =\ell_{\mathrm{PT}}(a)^{\prime}\Omega_x\ell_{\mathrm{PT}}(a).
 \tag{16}
\]
Feasibility follows from (12).  The feasible set is affine and closed, and its image in the finite-dimensional span of \(h_x\) is a closed affine subspace.  Projection of zero onto that subspace proves existence of a minimizing represented function.  Redundant coordinates may give several coefficient pairs, but all such pairs represent the same minimum-norm function; the Euclidean minimum-norm tie rule defines \((a_x^U,d_x^U)\).  The constant-rank and positive-spectrum assumptions ensure that the retained coordinate system is well defined and that no division is taken by a zero eigenvalue.

The stratum-supported functions are orthogonal across distinct \(x\), and \(p_X(x)\ge\kappa_0>0\).  Therefore the unconditional projection separates into the finite collection of programs, giving
\[
 \phi_U
 =\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a_x^U)
 =\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d_x^U),
 \qquad
 V_U(P_0)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_X(x)\min\mathrm{QP}_x.
 \tag{17}
\]

Finally, an estimator regular on \(\mathcal M_U\) is regular along every quadratic-mean differentiable submodel in either branch.  Its regular influence component must consequently satisfy both sets of derivative covariance equations, and hence belongs to the common class in (13).  Applying the regular-estimator variance bound in \(\mathrm{lem{:}semiparametric\text{-}convolution\text{-}bound}\) to finite collections of such branch submodels and then taking their closed span gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_0}(\text{regular limit})
 \ge \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\cap\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)}E_0[\phi^2]
 =E_0[\phi_U^2]=V_U(P_0).
 \tag{18}
\]
The bound is sharp as a tangent-experiment envelope because (17) exhibits the minimum-norm common derivative representer.  The cited result \(\mathrm{lem{:}sun\text{-}xie\text{-}zhang\text{-}branchwise\text{-}laws}\) supplies separate PT and SC laws and their possibly different variances; (17)--(18) give the additional bound imposed at an intersection by regularity to either identifying branch.

Retain the notation
\[
 \psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)=g_{\mathrm{PT},x}+R_{\mathrm{PT},x}^{\prime}a,
 \qquad
 \psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)=g_{\mathrm{SC},x}+R_{\mathrm{SC},x}^{\prime}d
 \tag{1}
\]
from the proof of \(\mathrm{thm{:}union\text{-}envelope}\).  The tangent normal form and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}oracle\text{-}gram\text{-}tests}\) give
\[
 \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\sum_x\psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a_x^{\mathrm{or}}),
 \qquad
 \phi_{\mathrm{SC}}=\sum_x\psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d_x^{\mathrm{or}}).
 \tag{2}
\]
The Euclidean tie rule affects only coordinates: each expression in (2) is the unique minimum-norm element of its affine influence-function class.

By disjoint stratum support and \(p_X(x)\ge\kappa_0>0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}-\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\|_{P_0}^2
 &=\sum_xp_X(x)
 E_0[\{\psi_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a_x^{\mathrm{or}})
       -\psi_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d_x^{\mathrm{or}})\}^2\mid X=x]\\
 &=\sum_xp_X(x)c(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x^{\mathrm{or}})^{\prime}
   \Omega_xc(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x^{\mathrm{or}}).
\end{aligned}
 \tag{3}
\]
The last expression is the simultaneous Gram discrepancy.  It is nonnegative, and it vanishes if and only if \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\) in \(L^2(P_{0,O})\).

Let
\[
 A=\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0),\qquad
 B=\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0),\qquad
 C=A\cap B.
 \tag{4}
\]
The normal form makes \(A\) and \(B\) closed affine subsets of \(\mathcal H_{P_0}\), because their direction spaces are finite-dimensional spans of restriction normals.  The union theorem gives \(C\ne\varnothing\), and \(C\) is closed and affine.  Since \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\) is the orthogonal projection of zero onto \(A\), for every \(c\in C\subseteq A\) the projection identity gives
\[
 \|c\|_{P_0}^2
 =\|\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\|_{P_0}^2
  +\|c-\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\|_{P_0}^2.
 \tag{5}
\]
Minimizing (5) over \(c\in C\) yields
\[
 V_U=V_{\mathrm{PT}}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\in C
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\in B.
 \tag{6}
\]
Using (1)--(2), the squared distance from \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\) to \(B\) is
\[
 \min_{(d_x)}\sum_xp_X(x)c(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x)^{\prime}
 \Omega_xc(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x).
 \tag{7}
\]
This finite positive-semidefinite quadratic program attains its minimum after redundant coordinates are removed, or equivalently under the Moore--Penrose convention.  Therefore (6) is equivalent to the PT-oracle discrepancy in (7) being zero.

Interchanging the two branches gives, by the same projection identity,
\[
 V_U=V_{\mathrm{SC}}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\in A
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \min_{(a_x)}\sum_xp_X(x)c(a_x,d_x^{\mathrm{or}})^{\prime}
 \Omega_xc(a_x,d_x^{\mathrm{or}})=0.
 \tag{8}
\]
This is exactly the SC-oracle discrepancy.

If \(V_U=V_{\mathrm{PT}}=V_{\mathrm{SC}}\), equations (6) and (8) put both branch canonical gradients in \(C\).  Each must then equal the unique projection of zero onto \(C\), so \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\).  Conversely, if those two gradients are equal, their common value lies in \(C\).  Every member of \(C\) belongs to each branch face and therefore has squared norm at least each branch minimum; the common branch minimizer itself belongs to \(C\), so all three minima equal its squared norm.  This proves simultaneous oracle adaptation.  Equation (3) proves its equivalent Gram test, while (7)--(8) prove the two one-sided tests.  Finally, every entry of these programs is a conditional second moment of the observed vector \(h_x\), and the finite-support probabilities are positive, so all three discrepancies are identified from \(P_{0,O}\).

There is one stratum and each group has probability \(1/3\).  Thus \(p_X(x)=1\ge\kappa_0\) and \(p_g(x)=1/3>\epsilon_0\), so the cell-mass and overlap conditions hold.  No anticipation holds by construction.  All three untreated final changes are zero, so conditional parallel trends holds and
\[
 D=(0,0)^{\prime},\quad
 \delta_1^0=0,\qquad
 q_{\mathrm{PT}}(P^{\star})
 =\delta_1^0\mathbf 1_2-D=(0,0)^{\prime}.
 \tag{1}
\]
The augmented donor matrix and treated preperiod target are
\[
 B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\\-2&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B^{\prime}B=\begin{pmatrix}6&-4\\-4&6\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The eigenvalues of \(B^{\prime}B\) are \(2\) and \(10\), hence the SC rank condition holds because \(\kappa_0<1\).  Solving \(Bw=a\) gives the unique weight vector
\[
 w=(1/2,1/2)^{\prime}.
 \tag{3}
\]
The same weights reproduce the treated untreated mean at period three, so the synthetic-mean restriction holds at every period.  Together with the assumed fourth-moment envelope, (1)--(3) prove \(P^{\star}\in\mathcal M_I\).  The envelope qualification is substantive: among the fixed untreated cells the largest fourth moment is \(68\), and the treated observed final fourth moment is \((\tau^{\star})^4+6(\tau^{\star})^2+1\); the proposition assumes that \(M_4\) dominates the relevant values.

For \(g,t\in\{1,2,3\}\), define the centered cell-mean influence variables
\[
 z_{g,t}=3\mathbf 1\{G=g\}\varepsilon_{g,t}.
 \tag{4}
\]
The independent centered innovations and disjoint group indicators make these nine variables pairwise orthogonal.  Their variances, listed by time within group, are
\[
 (3,3,3),\qquad (3,3/2,3/2),\qquad (6,6,6).
 \tag{5}
\]
In particular, the influence functions of the final changes of donors two and three have variances \(3\) and \(12\), respectively.  The PT normal changes the two donor weights subject to their sum being one.  For weights \((v,1-v)\), the donor portion of the variance is therefore
\[
 3v^2+12(1-v)^2.
 \tag{6}
\]
Its derivative is \(30v-24\) and its second derivative is \(30>0\), so its unique minimizer is \(v=4/5\).  The treated final-change contribution has variance \(3+3=6\).  Hence
\[
 V_{\mathrm{PT}}(P^{\star})
 =6+3(4/5)^2+12(1/5)^2
 =\frac{42}{5}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Moreover, \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}\) has rank one and the donor-change contrast has variance \(3+12=15>0\).  Thus the profiled PT normal has rank exactly one.

We now compute the SC face.  The vector \(u=(0,-2,1)^{\prime}\) spans \(\ker(B^{\prime})\) and satisfies \(u^{\prime}u=5\).  At the exact restriction, differentiation of the full-rank weight formula gives
\[
 \dot w=(B^{\prime}B)^{-1}B^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B\,w),
 \qquad
 -(-2,2)\dot w=(0,-2/5,-4/5)(\dot a-\dot B\,w).
 \tag{8}
\]
It follows that the unrestricted SC gradient has coefficients, ordered by time within groups one, two, and three,
\[
 (-2/5,-4/5,1),\qquad
 (1/5,2/5,-1/2),\qquad
 (1/5,2/5,-1/2).
 \tag{9}
\]
Normalize the one-dimensional SC normal as
\[
 \rho=u^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B\,w).
\]
Adding \(\beta\rho\) to (9) changes only preperiod coordinates.  Orthogonality in (5) gives its preperiod variance as
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q(\beta)
 &=3(-2/5-2\beta)^2+3(-4/5+\beta)^2
   +3(1/5+\beta)^2+\frac32(2/5-\beta/2)^2\\
 &\quad+6(1/5+\beta)^2+6(2/5-\beta/2)^2\\
 &=\frac{207}{8}\beta^2+\frac35\beta+\frac{99}{25}.
\end{aligned}
 \tag{10}
\]
The coefficient \(207/8\) is positive, so
\[
 \beta^{\mathrm{or}}=-\frac{4}{345},
 \qquad
 \min_{\beta}Q(\beta)=\frac{91}{23}.
 \tag{11}
\]
The final-period variance from (9) is
\[
 3+\frac14\frac32+\frac14 6=\frac{39}{8}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 V_{\mathrm{SC}}(P^{\star})
 =\frac{39}{8}+\frac{91}{23}
 =\frac{1625}{184}.
 \tag{12}
\]

Every SC normal is supported on preperiod mean coordinates, so every member of the SC influence face has final donor coefficients \((-1/2,-1/2)\).  Equality with a PT representative forces its donor weights to be \((1/2,1/2)\).  In (9)--(10), equality with that PT representative forces \(\beta^U=-1/5\): the treated preperiod coefficients become \((0,-1)\), each donor's preperiod coefficients become \((0,1/2)\), and the final coefficients are \((1,-1/2,-1/2)\).  The union theorem identifies this common representative as \(\phi_U\), and hence
\[
 V_U(P^{\star})
 =6+3(1/2)^2+12(1/2)^2
 =\frac{39}{4}.
 \tag{13}
\]
The inequalities \((1/2,1/2)\ne(4/5,1/5)\) and \(-1/5\ne-4/345\) show that neither branch oracle gradient belongs to the other branch face.  By \(\mathrm{thm{:}oracle\text{-}adaptation\text{-}frontier}\), both one-sided Gram discrepancies are strictly positive.  Direct subtraction of (7), (12), and (13) gives
\[
 V_U(P^{\star})-V_{\mathrm{PT}}(P^{\star})=\frac{27}{20},
 \qquad
 V_U(P^{\star})-V_{\mathrm{SC}}(P^{\star})=\frac{169}{184}.
 \tag{14}
\]
All entries of the finite Gram matrices are continuous functions of the cell probabilities, means, and second moments.  Positive cell masses, positive nonzero eigenvalues, unequal positive donor-change variances, unequal oracle weights, and the two strict gaps in (14) therefore persist in a sufficiently small neighborhood within \(\mathcal M_I\).  Intersecting that neighborhood with the fourth-moment envelope gives the asserted relatively open region, including when the envelope itself is met on its relative boundary.

If \(J=1\), then \(\mathbf 1_J\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}=1\), and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}restriction\text{-}maps}\) gives
\[
 A_{\mathrm{PT}}=I_1-1=0,
 \qquad
 r_{\mathrm{PT},x}=0.
 \tag{1}
\]
The tangent normal form therefore yields
\[
 \mathcal T_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)=\mathcal H_{P_0},
 \tag{2}
\]
and \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\) is the singleton \(\{\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\}\).  In particular, the SC tangent space is a subspace of the unrestricted PT observed tangent space.

It remains to verify the derivative compatibility, since equality of two functionals at only one law would not suffice.  With one donor, the intercept restriction forces \(w_2(x)=1\), and the SC restriction gives
\[
 \mu_{1,t}(x)=\mu_{2,t}(x),\qquad t<T.
 \tag{3}
\]
Thus at every nearby law in the SC branch,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \theta_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_O)
 &=\pi_1^{-1}\sum_xp_X(x)p_1(x)
 \{\mu_{1,T}(x)-\mu_{1,T-1}(x)-\mu_{2,T}(x)+\mu_{2,T-1}(x)\}\\
 &=\pi_1^{-1}\sum_xp_X(x)p_1(x)
 \{\mu_{1,T}(x)-\mu_{2,T}(x)\}
 =\theta_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_O),
\end{aligned}
 \tag{4}
\]
where the second equality uses (3) at \(t=T-1\).  Hence their derivatives agree along every SC tangent score.  Since \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\) represents the derivative of \(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}\) on all of \(\mathcal H_{P_0}\), equation (4) implies \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)\).  Therefore
\[
 \mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\subseteq\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0),
 \qquad
 \mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\cap\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)
 =\{\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\}.
 \tag{5}
\]
The definitions of \(\phi_U\) and \(V_U\) now give \(\phi_U=\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\) and \(V_U=V_{\mathrm{PT}}\).

For \(T=2\), write \(\Delta Y=Y_2-Y_1\) and
\[
 m_g(x)=E_O[\Delta Y\mid G=g,X=x].
\]
Overlap gives \(p_1(x)>0\), \(p_2(x)=1-p_1(x)>0\), and \(\pi_1>0\), so every division below is valid.  Direct differentiation of the PT observed-law functional gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}(O)
 &=\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=1\}}{\pi_1}\{\Delta Y-m_1(X)\}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=2\}}{\pi_1}\frac{p_1(X)}{p_2(X)}
   \{\Delta Y-m_2(X)\}\\
 &\quad+\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=1\}}{\pi_1}
 \{m_1(X)-m_2(X)-\theta\}.
\end{aligned}
 \tag{6}
\]
The first two residual terms have conditional mean zero.  The last term is centered because \(\theta=E_O[m_1(X)-m_2(X)\mid G=1]\), and it is the derivative contribution from the treated covariate distribution.  Thus (6) is mean zero and direct pathwise differentiation verifies its covariance equation for every unrestricted observed score.  Under the relabeling of treated and comparison indicators as \(G=1\) and \(G=2\), (6) is the panel-data ATT efficient influence function stated in \(\mathrm{lem{:}santanna\text{-}zhao\text{-}panel\text{-}did\text{-}gradient}\).

The obstruction is caused by the quantifiers in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}local\text{-}union\text{-}sequences}\), not by infeasibility of the center QP.  Choose the displayed margins so that \(P^{\star}\) satisfies the overlap, fourth-moment, rank, spectral-gap, and variance conditions with strict slack.  For a fixed sufficiently small \(\delta\ne0\), retain the donor means and every innovation law of \(P^{\star}\), but replace the treated untreated mean path by
\[
 (1/2+\delta)(-1,-2,-2)+(1/2-\delta)(1,2,2)
 =(-2\delta,-4\delta,-4\delta).
 \tag{1}
\]
Give the treated group the same additive final-period treatment effect as under \(P^{\star}\), and call the resulting law \(Q_\delta\).  The treated and both donor untreated final changes remain zero, so parallel trends holds.  The full-rank donor matrix is unchanged, and (1) is reproduced by the unique weights
\[
 w_\delta=(1/2+\delta,1/2-\delta)^{\prime}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus the synthetic-mean restriction also holds.  Group and stratum probabilities are unchanged, and all innovations remain bounded.  The structurally zero Gram directions persist, while the nonzero eigenvalues and the local-score variance vary continuously with \(\delta\).  The strict margins therefore continue to hold for all sufficiently small \(|\delta|\).  Hence \(Q_\delta\in\mathcal M_I\) and it satisfies every coordinatewise margin in the local-sequence definition.

Fix an integer \(m\).  Construct two triangular sequences.  In each, set the law at coordinate \(m\) equal to \(Q_\delta\) and every other coordinate equal to \(P^{\star}\).  Label coordinate \(m\) by PT in the first sequence and by SC in the second, using any admissible label elsewhere.  Each sequence belongs to \(\mathfrak L_U(P^{\star})\): after its single exceptional coordinate it is identically \(P^{\star}\), so its QMD expansion holds with score zero and remainder zero eventually, and both possible coordinate laws obey the fixed margins.  Thus, for every sample size \(m\), the supremum over the frozen sequence class contains two labeled copies of the same observed law \(Q_\delta\) at that coordinate.

At \(P^{\star}\), Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}strict\text{-}three\text{-}group\text{-}witness}\) shows that the common score has final donor coefficients \((-1/2,-1/2)\).  The PT chart extension freezes its normal coefficient at \(P^{\star}\), and the donor distributions are unchanged, so its final donor coefficients at \(Q_\delta\) remain \((-1/2,-1/2)\).  By contrast, an SC normal uses only preperiod coordinates, while (2) makes the final donor coefficients of the unrestricted SC gradient \((-1/2-\delta,-1/2+\delta)\).  Therefore, for
\[
 \Delta_\delta
 =\phi_U^{\mathrm{loc}}(Q_\delta;\mathrm{PT},P^{\star})
  -\phi_U^{\mathrm{loc}}(Q_\delta;\mathrm{SC},P^{\star}),
 \tag{3}
\]
the final-innovation component is \(\delta(z_{2,3}-z_{3,3})\).  Every remaining component uses other group-period innovations.  Independence makes it orthogonal to the displayed component.  The variance calculation in the witness proof therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta^2]
 &\ge\delta^2\{\operatorname{Var}_{Q_\delta}(z_{2,3})
                 +\operatorname{Var}_{Q_\delta}(z_{3,3})\}\\
 &=\delta^2\left(\frac32+6\right)
 =\frac{15}{2}\delta^2>0.
\end{aligned}
 \tag{4}
\]
Both chart extensions are sums of mean-zero gradient and normal representers, so \(E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta]=0\).

Suppose that one estimator satisfied the requested asymptotic-linear expansion uniformly over \(\mathfrak L_U(P^{\star})\) and over each admissible chart label.  Apply it at sample size \(m\) to the two sequences just constructed, coupling them through the identical iid sample from \(Q_\delta\).  The estimator and the causal target on the left side are identical in the two expansions.  Subtraction of the uniformly negligible remainders would therefore imply
\[
 S_m:=m^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^m\Delta_\delta(O_i)=o_{Q_\delta}(1).
 \tag{5}
\]
By iid sampling and centering,
\[
 E_{Q_\delta}[S_m^2]=E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta^2]
 \ge\frac{15}{2}\delta^2.
 \tag{6}
\]
Moreover, \(\Delta_\delta\) is a bounded linear combination of finitely many Rademacher innovations.  The standard fourth-moment expansion for independent centered summands gives
\[
 E_{Q_\delta}[S_m^4]
 =m^{-1}E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta^4]
  +3(1-m^{-1})E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta^2]^2,
 \tag{7}
\]

No estimator can therefore possess both chart expansions uniformly over the frozen sequence class.  Since the asymptotic-linear expansion is a required conjunct of the requested four-part attaining construction, that full affirmative result, including its variance-consistency and multiplier-coverage conclusions, is false under the frozen definition.
